summary: Describes the background behind removing the on-link assumption from IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. Under the original algorithm, a host with no default router assumed all destinations were on-link, which caused problems. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 used to say: if you know of no router, then everything must be on this cable. That helps in one odd case and hurts in several common ones, so it was removed. Now a host with no route to a destination says so straight away instead of trying to find it first.

subtitle: Why IPv6 Neighbor Discovery stopped assuming every destination is on the local link.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery told hosts that if they knew of no default router, then every destination must be on the local link. On a network with no IPv6 router that meant every IPv6 address had to be resolved on the link before the host could learn it was unreachable.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out four problems with the assumption: it can make address selection prefer an unreachable IPv6 address over a reachable IPv4 one, it adds at least three seconds of address resolution plus transport retransmission delays, it leaves the behaviour undefined on multi-interface hosts, and it creates a way to attack a host and to leak IPv6 traffic past a VPN.
tldr.outcome: The assumption was removed from the Neighbor Discovery specification in RFC 4861. A node with no route to a destination now sends an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable message instead of trying to resolve the address on the link.

ICMPv6 code for no route to destination

today: RFC 4943 is an Informational document published in September 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents a change that had already been made: the on-link assumption was removed from the Neighbor Discovery specification in RFC 4861.

sections.title: The Assumption and Why It Went
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery for IPv6 defines a conceptual sending algorithm for hosts. The version of that algorithm in RFC 2461 said that if a host's default router list is empty, the host assumes that all destinations are on-link. This memo records the removal of that assumption in the updated specification, RFC 4861, and sets out the reasons.

The assumption is problematic for IPv6-capable nodes that have no off-link IPv6 connectivity. That is typical when a system has IPv6 switched on at its network interfaces, either by default or by administrative configuration, and is attached to a network with no IPv6 service such as off-link routing. Such a system resolves DNS names to both AAAA and A records, and it may try to connect to unreachable IPv6 destinations off-link. The assumption creates problems for destination address selection, adds connection delays from unnecessary address resolution and neighbor unreachability detection, behaves in an undefined way on multi-interface nodes, and carries some subtle security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule said: if you know of no router, then every destination must be on this cable. That breaks the common case of a machine with IPv6 turned on sitting on a network that has no IPv6 at all, so it was taken out.

sections.title: Why the Assumption Existed
sections.content:
The assumption was created to make one particular scenario work: communication on a single link between systems configured with different global prefixes, in the absence of an IPv6 router. Consider two systems on separate links that have been manually configured with global addresses and are then plugged into each other back to back. They can still communicate over their global addresses, because each correctly assumes that the other is on-link. Without the assumption, that scenario would not work, and the systems would have to be configured to share a common prefix such as the link-local prefix.

The RFC's judgement is that the problems the assumption introduces outweigh the benefit it gives this one scenario, and that it is more beneficial to the end user to remove the assumption from Neighbor Discovery and declare this scenario illegitimate, in other words a misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: There was one good reason for the rule: two machines wired back to back, each with a different global address, could still talk if each assumed the other was local. The memo says that one odd case is not worth the trouble it causes everywhere else.

sections.title: Address Selection and the Delays It Caused
sections.content:
The first problem is the first rule of destination address selection. The algorithm in RFC 3484 takes an unordered list of destination addresses and produces a sorted one, and its first rule is "Avoid unusable destinations", which puts unreachable destinations at the end so that applications are least likely to try them first. The on-link assumption can produce false positives when an implementation decides whether a destination is unusable. On a network with no IPv6 router, where every off-link IPv6 destination is unreachable, an implementation could read the assumption as saying that an empty default router list means all destinations are reachable on-link. The result is that the rule prefers an unreachable IPv6 destination over a reachable IPv4 one.

The second problem is delay. Users expect applications to connect quickly to a destination regardless of how many IP addresses that destination has, so it matters that the system quickly determines that IPv6 destinations are unreachable and moves on to the others. With the assumption, a host on a network that has no IPv6 routers must perform link-layer address resolution on all IPv6 addresses to which it sends packets. The application does not receive acknowledgment of the unreachability of destinations that are not on-link until at least address resolution has failed, which takes no less than 3 seconds. Transport protocol delays amplify this greatly: RFC 1122 requires TCP to retransmit for at least 3 minutes before aborting the connection attempt. When the application holds a large list of off-link unreachable IPv6 addresses followed by at least one reachable IPv4 address, the delay before successful communication with the IPv4 address is unacceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical costs. The address sorting rule that puts unreachable addresses last could get it wrong, and pick a dead IPv6 address ahead of a working IPv4 one. And finding out that an IPv6 address is dead took at least three seconds, on top of however long the transport protocol keeps trying.

sections.title: Multi-Interface Ambiguity and Security Issues
sections.content:
The third problem is that the behaviour on a node attached to multiple links is undefined. The difficulty arises when a node has to send to an IPv6 destination for which it has no route: with the assumption it believes the destination is on-link, but on which link? An implementor has three choices. It can attempt to send the packet on a single link, either an administratively predefined one or one chosen by some algorithm. It can attempt to send the packet on every link. Or it can drop the packet.

If the destination really is on-link, the first choice might not succeed, because the wrong link could be picked. The second might reach the destination but is more complex to implement and is not guaranteed to pick the correct one: there could be more than one node configured with the same address, each reachable through a different link, and the address by itself does not disambiguate which destination the sender actually wanted. The third choice, dropping the packet, is equivalent to not making the assumption at all. In other words, if there is no route to the destination, do not attempt to send the packet, which requires an administrator to configure routes to the destination and so removes the ambiguity.

The fourth problem is security. The assumption introduces the vulnerability that RFC 3756 describes as "Default router is 'killed'": an attacker kills a host's router, so the host starts sending all its packets on-link, and the attacker can then spoof off-link nodes by sending packets on the same link as the host. The assumption also interacts badly with virtual private networks. It has been observed that some commercially available VPN software that does not support IPv6 does not simply drop IPv6 packets, but sends them to the local media in the clear. Consider a system with a single Ethernet interface and VPN software that encrypts and encapsulates certain packets: it resolves a name to an IPv6 address, and the packet ends up going in the clear to the local media, where a malicious third party can spoof the destination on-link.
sections.plainLanguage: With several network cards, the rule does not say which card to use, and the three possible answers are all bad. Worse, an attacker who knocks out your router can make you treat the whole Internet as being on your cable, where they can pretend to be anyone.

sections.title: What Changed in the Neighbor Discovery Specification
sections.content:
Three things changed between RFC 2461 and RFC 4861. The last sentence of the second paragraph of Section 5.2, the Conceptual Sending Algorithm, was removed: "If the Default Router List is empty, the sender assumes that the destination is on-link." Bullet item 3 in Section 6.3.6, Default Router Selection, was removed: "If the Default Router List is empty, assume that all destinations are on-link as specified in Section 5.2." And Appendix A was modified to remove the on-link assumption related text in bullet item 1 under the discussion of what happens when a multihomed host fails to receive Router Advertisements.

The result is that destinations are considered unreachable when there is no routing information for them, whether through a default router or otherwise. Instead of attempting link-layer address resolution when sending to such a destination, a node should send an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable message with code 0, no route to destination, up the stack. Section 5 states that removing the assumption addresses all of the security-related vulnerabilities of the protocol described earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: Three sentences were taken out of the specification. Now, if a host has no route to a destination, it reports that straight away with an ICMPv6 message instead of trying to find the destination on the local link.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PROBLEMS THE RFC LISTS

items.title: Address selection
items.text: An unreachable IPv6 address can be preferred over a reachable IPv4 one.

items.title: Delays
items.text: Every IPv6 address must be resolved on the link before the host learns it is unreachable.

items.title: Multi-interface ambiguity
items.text: Nothing says which link to use, and the behaviour is undefined.

items.title: Security
items.text: A killed router makes the host treat the whole Internet as local; VPNs can leak IPv6 packets.
